passage: Paulo spread two offer letters on a café table in Porto, next to his sister Dalia's laptop. He tried to stop staring at the salary lines. "Forget the numbers for a minute," he said quietly. "Where do I want to be in three years?" He answered himself: someone who can design systems, not only close tickets. Company A paid more, but its team was young and rushed, with nobody to look over his work. Company B paid less, yet it had Ines, a senior engineer who reviewed code line by line and taught juniors. "Who will teach me?" he said. "That matters more than the first year's package." Dalia refilled his coffee and said nothing. That evening he emailed Company B to accept.

qa.q: Who is the senior engineer at Company B?
qa.a: Ines is the senior engineer who reviewed code line by line.

qa.q: What is Paulo feeling as he tries to look past the salary lines?
qa.a: Paulo is torn but growing sure: he wants to become someone who can design systems, and that wish pulls him toward mentoring.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Paulo use to double-check his choice, and why?
qa.a: He could ask a current junior at Company B about the mentoring, because his values point to Ines but a junior can confirm whether teaching really happens.

qa.q: How does Dalia see Paulo's decision?
qa.a: Dalia sits beside him, refills his coffee and says nothing, which suggests she wants Paulo to reach the answer in his own words.

grounding: Shows values-first planning: asking what matters over three years and preferring the team with mentoring over a bigger starting package.

passage: In the placement office, Akash spread two offer letters on Ramesh Sir's desk. "Sir, one pays much more. The other has a better team. I keep flipping." Ramesh Sir pushed a blank sheet toward him. "Forget the letters for a minute. Where do you want to be in three years?" Akash thought. "Able to design a system on my own. Trusted with real work." "And who helps you get there?" Akash looked at the second letter. At that interview, the team lead had spent twenty minutes walking him through their code reviews and said, "I pair every new hire with me for the first six months." At the first company, he hadn't met anyone beyond HR. "The team with Meenakshi ma'am," Akash said slowly. "The package is lower, but she'll actually teach me." Ramesh Sir nodded. "Then that's your answer, not mine."

qa.q: What did the team lead say about new hires?
qa.a: I pair every new hire with me for the first six months.

qa.q: How did Akash feel before the question about three years?
qa.a: Akash felt torn and stuck, flipping between the higher pay and the better team.

qa.q: What else could Akash check before accepting?
qa.a: Akash could ask to speak with someone Meenakshi ma'am has mentored, to confirm the mentoring really happens.

qa.q: How does Ramesh Sir see his role?
qa.a: Ramesh Sir sees his job as asking the right question, not choosing, so he lets Akash reach the answer himself.

grounding: Shows a graduate asking what matters over the next three years and choosing mentoring and growth under a strong senior over a higher package.

passage:
Subject: I said yes to the smaller offer
Hi Vaibhav,
You asked why I didn't take the higher package. Here's my thinking.
I asked myself one question: what do I want to be able to do three years from now? My honest answer: build and ship a product feature end to end, and explain every decision in it.
Offer A pays about 30% more, but it's a support team, and nobody I met there writes code daily. Offer B has a senior engineer, Farooq, who has built two payment systems and told me he reviews every junior's code personally.
So I put mentoring and skill growth first and the package second. B won easily. I know A would feel nicer on payday. But in three years I think B makes me better at the work, and that matters more to me.
Tell me if I'm being naive.
Darshan

qa.q: How much more does Offer A pay?
How does Darshan feel about choosing the lower package?
qa.a: Darshan feels fairly confident but a little unsure too, asking Vaibhav whether it is naive.

qa.q: What else could Darshan confirm before joining?
qa.a: Darshan could ask B for a written plan of the first months, including how often Farooq's reviews happen.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav read the email?
qa.a: Vaibhav can see clear reasoning based on Darshan's three-year goal, and may reassure Darshan or point out anything missing.

grounding: Illustrates a graduate putting mentoring and skill growth ahead of a higher starting package and choosing the team with a strong senior engineer.
